project.name: agent
project.description: A Python LangGraph follow-up agent that watches job applications stuck in an early status (Applied/Screening) past a threshold, uses an LLM to draft polite follow-up emails parked for human approval, and sends them over SMTP once approved. It exposes a FastAPI API, runs a daily APScheduler cron, and shares a Postgres database and JWT identity with an ASP.NET backend.

tour.title: Architecture Overview
tour.description: There is no README, so ARCHITECTURE.md is the authoritative narrative and the right place to begin. It lays out the whole system at a glance: a nightly cron scans stale job applications, an LLM drafts a follow-up email, a human approves it, and only then is it sent over SMTP. Read this first to get the mental model of the assess -> human-review -> send flow and the single-process concurrency model that the rest of the tour will make concrete in code.

tour.title: Application Entry Point
tour.description: main.py is the composition root and the top of the dependency graph (highest fan-out in the project). It loads settings, builds a database connection factory, wires the LLM and mailer callbacks into the LangGraph, exposes the FastAPI app, and registers the nightly scheduled job. Everything the tour visits next is imported and assembled here, so this file is your map of how the pieces connect at runtime.
tour.languageLesson: This is a hand-rolled dependency-injection / composition root pattern: instead of modules reaching for globals, main.py constructs concrete dependencies (LLM client, mailer, DB factory) and passes them inward as callbacks. This keeps the workflow and persistence layers pure and easy to test with fakes.

tour.title: Configuration & Environment
tour.description: Before any logic runs, the app reads its entire runtime configuration from environment variables. config.py defines the Settings container and load_settings(), pulling in the Postgres DSN, LLM/OpenRouter credentials, JWT validation parameters, SMTP details, and the follow-up scheduling knobs. The paired .env.example is the template that documents every variable the agent expects, making it the fastest way to see what external systems this service depends on.

tour.title: Domain Model & Eligibility Rules
tour.description: This is the semantic core of the project. models.py defines the three data shapes that flow through the whole system: AppRow (a job application record), Draft (the LLM's proposed email), and FollowUpState (the state carried through the agent graph). rules.py is pure, side-effect-free logic that decides which applications are stale enough to warrant a follow-up and don't already have one. Understanding these two files unlocks every later step, since the graph, batch runner, and database all speak in these terms.
tour.languageLesson: rules.eligible_apps is deliberately pure: it takes data in and returns a filtered list with no I/O. Isolating business rules from database and network side effects is what lets test_rules.py exhaustively check boundary thresholds without a database.

tour.title: Persistence Layer
tour.description: db.py is the only module that talks to Postgres. It initializes the schema and provides CRUD queries for candidate applications and follow-up rows, including the row-locking read used during approval to prevent double-sends. A critical design point from the architecture: every query is scoped by user_id, since identity comes from a JWT shared with the ASP.NET backend and each user must only ever see their own applications and drafts.
tour.languageLesson: SQL row-level locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) is used here so that when a user approves a follow-up, the row is locked for the duration of the transaction. This guards the approval flow against a concurrent request sending the same email twice.

tour.title: The Agent Workflow Graph
tour.description: graph.py builds the heart of the system: a LangGraph state machine with three nodes -- assess (draft the email), human_review (interrupt and park for approval), and send (dispatch the email). Building on the FollowUpState model from Step 4, the graph routes conditionally: unwarranted applications end quietly, while warranted ones hit the human_review interrupt and are checkpointed in Postgres until a human resumes them. This interrupt-and-resume pattern is what makes the whole 'draft now, approve later' architecture possible.
tour.languageLesson: LangGraph's interrupt mechanism suspends the graph mid-execution and persists its state via a checkpointer (here, Postgres). Execution can resume much later -- even in a different process, triggered by an API call -- by passing a Command that tells the graph whether the human approved or rejected.

tour.title: LLM Drafting
tour.description: llm.py is the assess node's engine. It prompts a chat model through ChatOpenAI/OpenRouter with structured output, asking it two things at once: whether a follow-up is even warranted, and if so, what the subject and body should be. The structured response is mapped directly into the Draft model from Step 4, keeping the boundary between 'unpredictable LLM text' and 'typed domain object' clean and testable.
tour.languageLesson: Structured output constrains the LLM to return data matching a schema rather than free-form prose. This turns an inherently fuzzy model call into a reliable function that yields a typed Draft, so downstream code never has to parse loose text.

tour.title: Nightly Batch & Scheduler
tour.description: These two files drive the automated side of the system. batch.run_batch fetches candidate applications, filters them through rules.eligible_apps (Step 4), runs each through the agent graph (Step 6), and persists the resulting drafts. scheduler.py is a thin helper that registers run_batch as a nightly APScheduler cron job. Critically, all graph invocations are serialized behind a single process lock -- the concurrency model called out in Step 1's architecture doc.
tour.languageLesson: APScheduler registers time-based jobs inside the running process. Because the batch and the API share one process and one graph, a process-level lock serializes all graph.invoke calls, trading throughput for a simple, race-free correctness guarantee.

tour.title: API Layer & Identity
tour.description: api.py exposes the human-facing side: FastAPI endpoints to list parked follow-ups and to approve or reject them. auth.py is the gatekeeper, verifying the bearer JWT against the configured signing key, issuer, and audience -- the same token minted by the ASP.NET backend -- and extracting the user id that scopes every database query from Step 5. Approving a row resumes the checkpointed LangGraph (Step 6) via a Command, flowing execution into the send node.
tour.languageLesson: Sharing a JWT across two services (ASP.NET issues, this Python agent validates) means neither service needs its own login flow. The Python side only needs the signing key, issuer, and audience to trust tokens the .NET backend already issued, keeping identity centralized.

tour.title: AI Résumé & JD Sub-Router
tour.description: The FastAPI sub-router mounted under the API layer that powers the AI features: storing a user's résumé, extracting structured data from a pasted job description, scoring a résumé against a JD, and generating an optimized résumé. It delegates model calls to the LLM module and persistence to the DB module.

tour.title: Sending the Email
tour.description: mailer.py is the final node in the workflow and the system's only outbound side effect. Once a human approves a draft and the graph resumes into its send node, send_email builds an EmailMessage and dispatches it over a STARTTLS-authenticated SMTP connection using the settings from Step 3. This is the payoff of the entire assess -> review -> send pipeline: a real follow-up email leaves the building only after a human said yes.

tour.title: Runtime Stack & Dependencies
tour.description: requirements.txt pins the libraries that make everything above work: FastAPI and Uvicorn for the API, LangGraph/LangChain for the agent state machine, APScheduler for the nightly cron, psycopg for Postgres, and PyJWT for token validation. Reading this list ties the abstract architecture back to concrete technology choices and confirms this is a single, self-contained Python service rather than a sprawl of microservices.

tour.title: The Test Suite
tour.description: The project has a test module mirroring nearly every source file, which is the best documentation of intended behavior. test_graph.py verifies the interrupt/approve/reject paths of the workflow, test_rules.py pins down the eligibility boundaries, test_api.py covers JWT enforcement and the approve/reject endpoints, and test_batch.py confirms drafts are created only for warranted applications. Together they show how the pure, dependency-injected design from Step 2 pays off: fakes and monkeypatching stand in for the LLM, SMTP, and database.
tour.languageLesson: pytest fixtures (see conftest.py) provide a rolled-back Postgres connection per test and auto-skip when no database is present. Combined with monkeypatch to swap in fake LLM and SMTP clients, the suite exercises real logic while staying fast and hermetic.
